source.title: SAEs Discover Meaningful Features in the IOI Task

record.file_problem: The supplied post is readable and appears complete, but referenced plots are not included, so their plotted values cannot be extracted.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether SAE features in GPT2-Small support feature editing and resemble supervised features, extending the feature-recovery question to an LLM and a task-specific SAE evaluation.
record.gate_note: The post reports outcomes for SAE feature edits, their similarity to supervised features, and correlations between training metrics and edit success. It also describes the supervised-edit and no-intervention comparisons. Training details and the IOI task setup are not result rows.
record.test_reason: The post asks whether SAEs trained on IOI activations in GPT2-Small recover features that match supervised IOI attributes, judged by edit accuracy and cosine similarity. That bears on V4 (a dictionary recovers sparse features in a real LLM). It also bears partly on V5, since the features don't map one-to-one to the attributes.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say SAEs trained on IOI data, chosen with a cheap search on the editing test, nearly match supervised features for steering. Gated SAEs beat vanilla SAEs across the board, and topk (k=3) beats gated in most cases. Sparsity predicts edit success better than loss recovered. SAE features don't map one-to-one onto the supervised attributes: Pos looks split, and gated SAEs resemble the supervised features less.
record.recipe_differences: The post evaluates SAE feature editing and similarity in GPT2-Small on IOI; it does not reproduce the original toy-network setup or its sparsity-dependent geometric transition.
record.method_sensitivity: Editing method affects performance; topk's comparison with gated SAEs has an exception for interpretation-aware IO editing. Results also differ by attribute: IO features show significant similarity to supervised features, while Pos features do not show high similarity.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 56 checkpoints per site, lower ℓ0 tracks edit success (by a distance proxy) better than logit-difference recovered does.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard SAE training metrics predict SAEs' causal usefulness for editing only imperfectly; sparsity predicts it better than loss recovered.

record.problems: The supplied text omits the referenced plots and their numerical values. The post reports a single model and a narrow task, describes activation-distance as a proxy for edit success, and says it did not ablate the training improvements to determine which ingredients caused the gains. No uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No separately described result was left out. Numerical values from referenced plots could not be extracted because the plots are absent from the supplied text.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
No test of the capacity account of polysemanticity.
No test of other causes of polysemanticity.
No measure of how widely features are distributed across neurons. Only one model and one narrow task, with SAEs trained on task data.
No test of stability across seeds, of completeness, or of whether SAEs trained on a general distribution behave the same way.
No comparison of one-dimensional and multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: The S attribute was dropped from the evaluation because no-intervention scores nearly as well as supervised edits. Footnote: (S,Pos) and (IO,Pos) pair attributes ended up 'simulating' the three-attribute features.

record.verdict_notes: This is a blog follow-up to arXiv:2405.08366. All key values are only in plots absent from the text. The SAEs were trained on task-specific IOI data and picked by their editing performance, so the selection overlaps with the evaluation. There are no uncertainty estimates, and the training ingredients were not ablated.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from competition for limited capacity or important features receiving dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
Does not establish how widespread these representations are across LLMs, tasks, or features, or measure feature distribution across neurons.
Does not test feature stability across training runs or contexts, or establish completeness or canonical status.
Does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional feature representations as accounts of superposition.

rows.subject: GPT2-Small
rows.operation_detail: Compared SAE features with supervised features using mean max cosine similarity.
rows.measure: Mean max cosine similarity to supervised IO features
rows.value: figure only; text says similarities are significant
rows.locator: Are The SAE Features Similar To The Supervised Features?
rows.note: The post interprets this as evidence that the SAEs picked up features close to supervised IO features.
rows.check: Subject note: the SAEs were trained on IOI prompts only, and were selected by the editing test itself (choice of L1 penalty and checkpoint). Both limit how far this generalizes to recovery in general.

source_check.correct: Mean-max cosine similarity is computed for each IOI circuit site and attribute, rather than stated to be averaged across sites. IO similarities support observed for V4; correspondence with supervised features cannot determine completeness, stability or canonicity under V5.
source_check.locator_found: Are The SAE Features Similar To The Supervised Features?, lines 145–149; supervised-feature caveat, line 49.
source_check.problem: The aggregation condition is incorrect, and the observed state is unsupported for the V5 link.

source_check.correct: Mean-max cosine similarity is computed for each IOI circuit site and attribute. Pos similarities are low, and splitting is a suspected explanation. Partial recovery relative to supervised Pos features bears on V4; V5 is cannot_determine because the supervised attributes are not established as canonical model units.

rows.subject: GPT2-Small
rows.operation_detail: Compared gated SAE features with supervised features using mean max cosine similarity.
rows.measure: Mean max cosine similarity to supervised features
rows.value: figure only; text says gated SAEs, which edit more successfully, have somewhat lower similarities to supervised features
rows.locator: Are The SAE Features Similar To The Supervised Features?
rows.note: The authors suggest this may indicate structure not captured by their supervised features.
rows.check: Gated SAEs edit better but resemble the supervised features less. This bears on the canonical-unit question (V5), not on whether features are recoverable (V4), so drop V4.

relationships.condition: Gated and topk SAEs trained on IOI activations in GPT2-Small, interpretation-agnostic two-feature edits, IO attribute
relationships.reason: Gated edits come close to or exceed supervised edit accuracy at reasonable edit precision (r2, r3). IO SAE features have significant cosine similarity to the supervised features (r9). Topk with k=3 generally does better still (r5).
relationships.display_finding: Gated SAE edits came close to or exceeded supervised edit accuracy at reasonable precision, and topk with k=3 generally did better. IO SAE features had significant cosine similarity to the supervised features.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Gated and topk SAEs trained on IOI activations in GPT2-Small, interpretation-agnostic two-feature edits, IO attribute
source_check.reason: Near-supervised editing with limited feature exchange and substantial IO cosine similarity provide indirect recovery evidence in this setting (r2, r3, r9); the topk comparison supplies further qualified support (r5).

relationships.condition: Vanilla SAEs, interpretation-aware feature selection, and the Pos attribute
relationships.reason: Vanilla SAEs lag significantly in edit accuracy (r1). Selecting features by interpretation costs non-trivial accuracy (r4). Pos is matched poorly (r10). Recovery depends on SAE architecture and selection method.
relationships.display_finding: Vanilla SAEs lagged significantly in edit accuracy, and selecting features by their interpretation cost non-trivial accuracy. The Pos attribute was matched poorly.

source_check.condition: Vanilla SAEs, interpretation-aware feature selection, and the Pos attribute

relationships.condition: Gated and vanilla SAEs on IOI in GPT2-Small
relationships.reason: The Pos attribute appears split across several SAE features (r10). The better-editing gated SAEs resemble the supervised features less (r11). So SAE features don't correspond one-to-one with the task's attributes.
relationships.display_finding: The Pos attribute appeared split across several SAE features, and the gated SAEs that edited better resembled the supervised features less.
